en: Majjhima Nikāya 7 Vatthasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were a cloth that was soiled and stained with dirt.”
Whatever dye a dyer might apply to it—whether blue, yellow, red, or madder—it would remain poorly colored and impure in color.
Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks.
"In the same way, monks, when the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected.
Just as, monks, there might be a cloth that is pure and bright;
whatever dye a dyer were to apply to it—whether blue, yellow, red, or magenta—it would take on a beautiful color, a pure color.
For what reason?
Because of the purity of the cloth, monks.
In the same way, monks, when the mind is undefiled, a happy destination is to be expected.
And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind?
Covetousness and improper greed are a defilement of the mind; ill will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind;
resentment is a defilement of the mind; contempt is a defilement of the mind; disparagement is a defilement of the mind.
Corruption: envy is a corruption of the mind, stinginess is a corruption of the mind, deceit is a corruption of the mind,
fraudulence is a corruption of the mind, obstinacy is a corruption of the mind, aggression is a corruption of the mind,
conceit is a corruption of the mind, arrogance is a corruption of the mind, and intoxication [is a corruption of the mind].
“Negligence is a corruption of the mind; negligence is a corruption of the mind.
Having understood, ‘Covetousness and improper greed are corruptions of the mind,’ that bhikkhu abandons covetousness and improper greed as a corruption of the mind;
having understood, ‘Ill will is a corruption of the mind’...”
Having understood this, one abandons ill will as an imperfection of the mind;
having understood that “anger is an imperfection of the mind,” one abandons anger as an imperfection of the mind.
‘Resentment is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, he abandons resentment as a defilement of the mind;
‘Spite is a defilement of the mind’—
Having understood this, one abandons hypocrisy as a defilement of the mind;
having understood that "contempt is a defilement of the mind," one abandons contempt as a defilement of the mind.
‘Envy is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, he abandons envy as a defilement of the mind; ‘Avarice is a defilement of the mind’— [having understood this, he abandons avarice as a defilement of the mind].
Having understood this, one abandons the defilement of the mind that is stinginess;
having understood that "deceit is a defilement of the mind," one abandons the defilement of the mind that is deceit.
“Deceit is a defilement of the mind”—
having understood this, he abandons deceit as a defilement of the mind; “Arrogance is a defilement of the mind”— [having understood this, he abandons arrogance as a defilement of the mind].
Having understood this, one abandons rigidity as a defilement of the mind;
having understood that "aggression is a defilement of the mind," one abandons aggression as a defilement of the mind.
‘Conceit is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, he abandons conceit as a defilement of the mind;
‘Excessive conceit is a defilement of the mind’—
Having understood this, one abandons excessive conceit, a defilement of the mind;
having understood that "intoxication is a defilement of the mind," one abandons intoxication, a defilement of the mind.
‘Negligence is a defilement of the mind’— having understood this, one abandons negligence as a defilement of the mind.

But when, monks, for a bhikkhu ‘covetousness and unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’— having understood this, covetousness and unrighteous greed as a defilement of the mind have been abandoned.
‘Ill will is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, ill will as a defilement of the mind is abandoned;
‘Anger is a defilement of the mind’—
Having understood this, anger, a defilement of the mind, is abandoned;
having understood that "resentment is a defilement of the mind," resentment, a defilement of the mind, is abandoned.
‘Deceit is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, deceit as a defilement of the mind is abandoned;
‘Conceit is a defilement of the mind’— having understood this...
Having understood this, the corruption of the mind that is envy is abandoned;
having understood, ‘Envy is a corruption of the mind,’ the corruption of the mind that is envy is abandoned.
‘Avarice is an affliction of the mind’—
having understood this, avarice as an affliction of the mind is abandoned;
‘Deceit is an affliction of the mind’—
Having understood this, deceit as a defilement of the mind is abandoned;
having understood that "crookedness is a defilement of the mind," crookedness as a defilement of the mind is abandoned.
‘Arrogance is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, arrogance as a defilement of the mind is abandoned;
‘hostility is a defilement of the mind’—
Having understood this, the mental corruption of agitation is abandoned;
having understood that "conceit is a mental corruption," conceit as a mental corruption is abandoned.
‘Conceit is a defilement of the mind’—
having understood this, conceit as a defilement of the mind is abandoned;
‘Intoxication is a defilement of the mind’—
Having understood this, intoxication, a defilement of the mind, is abandoned;
having understood that "negligence is a defilement of the mind," negligence, a defilement of the mind, is abandoned.
Thus he is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha:

"The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves’;
he possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:

‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the straight way, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the true way...’
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing rightly;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples consists of these four pairs of persons, these eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’”

Furthermore, when what has been gained by him has been relinquished, vomited out, released, abandoned, and cast aside, he gains the knowledge of the meaning, "I am possessed of verified confidence in the Buddha"; he gains the knowledge of the Dhamma;
and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
Thinking, "I am endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma... and in the Saṅgha," one gains knowledge of the goal, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is glad, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Furthermore, thinking, "To the extent that it was possible, I have abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and let go of it," one gains the knowledge of the goal, gains the knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains the joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is glad, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

“Monks, when a monk is of such virtue, such a nature, and such wisdom, even if he eats almsfood made of fine rice—free of black grains, served with many soups and many condiments—that does not become an obstacle for him.
Just as a cloth that is soiled and stained becomes pure and bright through contact with clear water, or as gold becomes pure and bright when brought to the mouth of a furnace;”

In the same way, monks, when a monk of such virtue, such Dhamma, and such wisdom eats almsfood made of fine rice, with the black grains removed, accompanied by many soups and many curries, that does not become an obstacle for him.
He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.
Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will;
with a mind accompanied by compassion …pe… with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe…
He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus he understands: "This exists; there is the inferior; there is the superior; there is an escape beyond this realm of perception.

For him who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, monks, is called a monk who is bathed with the inner bath.”
Now at that time, the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Does the venerable Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe?”
“What, brahmin, is the use of the Bāhukā River? What will the Bāhukā River do?

“For many people, Master Gotama, the Bāhukā River is considered a place for bathing; for many people, Master Gotama, the Bāhukā River is considered a source of merit; moreover, many people wash away their evil deeds in the Bāhukā River.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja with verses:
“Bāhuka, Adhikakka,
Gaya, and also Sundarika;”
The Sarassatī, the Payāgā,
and also the river Bāhumatī—
the fool constantly leaps into these.
One who has black karma is not purified.
What can Sundarikā do?
What can the Payāga or the Bāhukā river do?
For a person who has committed evil deeds and performed wicked acts,
no one can ever purify that doer of sin.
For the pure, indeed, it is always springtime.
For one who is pure, the Uposatha is always [fulfilled];
for one who is pure and of clean deeds,
the vow is always successfully accomplished.
Bathe right here, O brahmin;
bring security to all living beings.
If you do not speak falsehood, [you have bathed].
If you do not harm living beings,
if you do not take what is not given,
if you have faith and are free from stinginess;
"What will you achieve by going to Gayā?
Even this well is your Gayā.
When this was said, the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [even so has this Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways].”
"In this very way, Master Gotama, the Dhamma has been proclaimed by you in many ways.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive full ordination."
The brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Not long after his full ordination, the venerable Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time attained that goal for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
He dwelt having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life, entering upon and abiding therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And thus the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the Arahants.
The Vatthasutta, the seventh, is finished.
